links.title: How is failed replication handled?
links.body: SILO queues failed replication operations and retries those operations until replication succeeds.

links.title: What are Replication Workers?
links.body: SILO uses a replication queuing system with multiple concurrent replication workers operating on that queue.

links.title: How is Erasure Coding used to Protect Data?
links.body: SILO erasure coding is a data redundancy and  availability feature that allows SILO deployments to  automatically reconstruct objects on-the-fly despite  the loss of multiple drives or nodes in the cluster.

links.title: Recover After Hardware failure
links.body: Depending on the deployment topology and  selected erasure code parity, SILO can tolerate loss  of up to half the drives or nodes in the deployment  while maintaining read access to objects.

links.title: Site Failure Recovery
links.body: SILO can make the loss of an entire site, while  significant, a relatively minor incident. Site recovery depends on the replication option you use for the site.

links.title: Node Failure Recovery
links.body: If a SILO node suffers complete hardware failure, the node begins healing operations once it rejoins the  deployment.

links.title: What is SILO Healing?
links.body: Healing is SILO’s ability to restore data after some event causes data loss. Data loss can come from bit rot, drive loss, or node loss.

links.title: Understand SILO Healing Using mc
links.body: The mc admin heal command scans for objects that are damaged or corrupted and heals those objects.

links.title: What is Bit Rot?
links.body: Bit rot is data corruption that occurs without the user’s knowledge. SILO combats bit rot with hashing and erasure coding.

links.title: Overview of MinIO Erasure Coding
links.body: Through this MinIO video you will learn about MinIO erasure coding, including erasure sets, erasure parity, and stripe size. You will also learn about how the Reed-Solomon algorithm can be optimized for storage efficiency (yielding cost savings) or data lost protection (number of servers and drives that can fail). The video also walks through the MinIO Erasure Code calculator, considerations for cluster design and the command line syntax needed to establish an erasure code deployment.

links.title: What is the Scanner?
links.body: One of several low-priority processes SILO runs to check lifecycle management rules, bucket or site replication status, as well as object bit rot and healing

links.title: Lifecycle Management Object Scanner Considerations
links.body: SILO uses a scanner process to check objects against all configured lifecycle management rules. High IO workloads or limited system resources may delay application of lifecycle management rules

links.title: User Management
links.body: Each user can have one or more assigned policies that explicitly list the actions and resources to which that user has access. Users can also inherit policies from the groups in which they have membership.

links.title: Active Directory / LDAP Access Management
links.body: For identities managed by the external AD/LDAP provider, SILO uses the user’s Distinguished Name and attempts to map it against an existing policy.

links.title: LDAP Configuration

links.title: Policy Variables
links.body: SILO supports using policy variables for automatically substituting context from the authenticated user and/or the operation into the user’s assigned policy or policies.

links.title: OIDC Configuration
links.body: SILO supports using an OpenID Connect (OIDC) compatible IDentity Provider (IDP) such as Okta, KeyCloak, Dex, Google, or Facebook for external management of user identities.

links.title: Object Locking
links.body: SILO Object Locking (“Object Retention”) enforces Write-Once Read-Many (WORM) immutability to protect versioned objects from deletion.

links.title: Encryption
